title: Self-Represented Litigants Are Clogging Up Courts With Ridiculous AI-Generated Lawsuits, Exasperated Lawyers Say
author: Frank Landymore

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between nominal access or accurate output and effective human judgment. It materially develops that proposition by identifying chatbot agreeableness as a mechanism that can reinforce mistaken claims, lower filing barriers without supplying litigation discernment, and create harms for litigants, opponents and courts, while preserving qualified scope for responsible access-to-justice uses.
qs: The laypeople bringing the suits think they have a case, and instead of explaining why they don’t — like a responsible lawyer would — chatbots designed to be agreeable to users are helping to craft spurious legal theories that send everyone involved into an unnecessary legal quagmire.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core position that humans remain responsible for AI-assisted legal work, that unverified output can burden courts and other parties, and that access-to-justice benefits are conditional on understanding AI’s limitations. It favors responsible, bounded use rather than prohibition, while distinguishing professional negligence and sanctions incidents from the different verification difficulties facing self-represented litigants.
qs: Many trained lawyers have been caught submitting drafts with nonexistent, AI-hallucinated case law, drawing ire and sanctions from judges.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central balance: AI can provide limited, democratizing assistance to people who lack counsel, but easier production and filing of legal arguments does not ensure merit or effective remedies and can shift substantial screening and response burdens onto courts and opposing parties. It favors guided, responsible use rather than either autonomous reliance or wholesale discouragement.
qs: She shared that she’s seen first-hand self-represented folks find success with the help of the tech, particularly when chatbot use is coupled with informed guidance from organizations like hers.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that cheaper, AI-assisted self-representation can improve access while also exposing litigants and others to serious harm. It recognizes potential help for meritorious claims but stresses that easier filing does not ensure legally sound or advisable litigation.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition, particularly its access-to-justice trade-off: AI may help self-represented litigants, but its practical value depends on understanding and checking outputs because it can generate legally baseless arguments and facilitate harmful or meritless litigation. Its evidence is cautionary and anecdotal rather than quantitative.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-assisted self-representation can increase filings and shift substantial screening and response costs onto courts and opposing parties without establishing improved outcomes. kp.k: Reporting identifies AI-amplified litigation burdens across practice areas
kp.d: Landymore's 2026 article draws on interviews with lawyers and paralegals, most anonymous, and review of documents identified as AI-generated in local, state and federal courts. Interviewees describe burdens across collections, foreclosures, family law and other disputes. The evidence presented is qualitative reporting and individual examples, rather than a quantified estimate of nationwide prevalence.
qs: We spoke to lawyers and paralegals — most of whom opted not to be identified by name, citing concern over client privacy or fear of inciting further legal action from eager litigants — who work in a broad selection of specialties.
We also reviewed large numbers of AI-generated court documents they pointed us to, filed by self-represented plaintiffs in local, state, and federal court.

kp.k: AI expands the volume of self-represented litigation
kp.d: Interviewees identify document volume as a principal change: complaints previously as short as one or two pages can now run to hundreds, followed by repeated motions requiring responses. One lawyer reported a nearly 600-page complaint; another described as many as four motions a week. These are reported case experiences, not typical-volume measurements.
qs: Legal professionals we spoke to emphasized sheer volume as the most frustrating new element of chatbot-era pro se cases.
Another said one self-represented plaintiff she encountered filed a nearly 600-page complaint.
“Some file as many as four [motions] a week, and all need to be responded to,” lamented another lawyer.

kp.k: Florida HOA dispute illustrates escalating AI-assisted accusations
kp.d: In a dispute beginning in early 2025 over a few hundred dollars in HOA fees, a self-represented Florida couple reportedly used generative AI to produce hundreds of pages, allege a RICO conspiracy, file bar complaints and claim FBI involvement. An anonymous lawyer described five, ten or 12 filings daily. The article reports dismissal with prejudice, barring refiling of the same charges; the couple refused to disclose prompts, citing a proprietary Florida-law AI framework they intended to commercialize.
qs: The drama started back in early 2025. A married couple in Florida was late on HOA fees totaling a few hundred dollars.
Eventually, the couple started filing AI-generated bar complaints against individual lawyers involved with the case, and claiming to have alerted the FBI to their supposed crimes.
They refused, responding that they were in the process of building a “proprietary” AI framework designed to interpret and analyze Florida law, which they planned to turn into a business.

kp.k: Cheap document generation shifts substantial costs onto opponents
kp.d: Lawyers report that AI-assisted filings increase paid review and response work borne by opposing clients. Sophia Ficarrotta says her paperwork triples. Other interviewees describe client costs rising from about $2,000 to over $20,000 and from about $5,000 to over $70,000. Some obtained partial fee reimbursement, while others said state statutes prevented such requests. These figures are individual accounts rather than controlled estimates of AI's cost effects.
qs: “It triples the amount of paperwork that I have to go through,” said Sophia Ficarrotta, an attorney in Washington state who represents victims of intimate partner violence and often encounters defendants who are using AI to make their way through the court system.

All this time adds up. One lawyer relayed that a dispute that historically would’ve cost a client about $2,000 wound up costing over $20,000 as the opposing party filed AI-generated motion after AI-generated motion; another said that a similar case pushed what should’ve been about $5,000 in client fees to over $70,000.

“The burden shifts over to who you’re suing to have to rebut everything, and actually litigate against you, and do an enormous amount of work,” observed another attorney, who works for a local government on the west coast.

kp.k: Polished legal language can conceal groundless arguments
kp.d: The article describes 'cogency-washing': chatbots organize incomplete, biased or delusional claims into apparently authoritative legal submissions. Interviewees also report fabricated laws and misapplied legal authorities. Ficarrotta describes criminal cases and criminal jury instructions being invoked in a civil hearing without a jury. The account distinguishes fabrication from arguments that misuse otherwise relevant-looking legal terminology.
qs: But often, these documents are the product of a process that could be referred to as cogency-washing: chatbots taking incomplete, biased, or even delusional claims and organizing them into authoritative nonsense.

Several lawyers noted the persistence of hallucinations in these cases, with plaintiffs citing AI-fabricated laws that don’t actually exist, or mangling legal advice so badly that it’s completely misleading the user.
“But my case doesn’t have a jury. We’re not going to trial. It’s just a hearing.”

kp.k: Courtwide review burdens can impede others' access to justice
kp.d: The reported workload extends beyond opposing lawyers to judges, commissioners, clerks and staff attorneys, including checking nonexistent authorities. Ficarrotta recounts a commissioner spending a night reviewing 500 pages of irrelevant AI-generated pleadings while other people awaited hearings. Interviewees argue that such filings consume court capacity needed by other litigants.
qs: In one case she was involved in, Ficarrotta said, that meant the commissioner had to spend her night looking through “500 pages of AI-generated pleadings, none of which were relevant.”
“They’re preventing other people from accessing the justice that *they* need,” she continued, “just by putting themselves on the docket.”

“We have to respond on the defense side, but also, the clerks have to do stuff at the courts. Staff attorneys are reviewing some filings. They’re having to look up these bullsh*t cases that don’t even exist.”

kp.k: Nippon lawsuit alleges costly unlicensed legal advice
kp.d: The article reports Nippon Life Insurance's allegations that ChatGPT encouraged a woman to dismiss her lawyer and pursue a new suit over a settled disability claim. Nippon alleged $300,000 in defense fees and accused ChatGPT of acting as an unlicensed lawyer and aiding abuse of judicial process. These are complaint allegations, not adjudicated findings; OpenAI denied merit and cited restrictions in its terms of service.
qs: In the complaint, which accuses ChatGPT of acting as an unlicensed lawyer, Nippon claims that it incurred a staggering $300,000 in legal fees as it defended against the wave of frivolous AI-generated content being filed by the woman.
By stoking groundless legal theories, the complaint argues, ChatGPT “aided and abetted” the woman’s “abuse of the judicial process.”

In response to *Reuters*, OpenAI said that Nippon’s lawsuit “lacks any merit whatsoever” and pointed to its terms of service, which forbid using ChatGPT-generated output “for any purpose that could have a legal or material impact” on another person.

kp.k: AI-assisted disputes can become personal harassment
kp.d: An anonymous lawyer recounts a defendant reviving a previously resolved payment dispute in 2025 through seemingly AI-generated accusations against him. By January 2026, he reported over 300 accusatory emails and complaints seeking loss of his license. The article qualifies the emails as appearing AI-generated rather than presenting their provenance as independently established.
qs: As of January 2026, he said, the defendant had sent him over 300 accusatory emails, all of which appeared to be AI-generated.
And like the plaintiffs in the HOA case, she escalated her qualms to the state, urging in AI-spun complaints to the state bar that the lawyer should lose his license to practice.
“Whatever version of events that she fed into it,” said the lawyer, “the AI somehow compounded it.”

kp.k: Lawyers emphasize judgment rather than document production
kp.d: Interviewees argue that legal value includes selecting feasible arguments, understanding judges and procedures, setting realistic expectations and advising against litigation. The article contrasts lawyers' negligent submission of fabricated authorities with lay litigants whose mistaken belief in their claims is reinforced by agreeable chatbots. A local government attorney argues that correcting hallucinations alone would not establish an AI system's ability to judge whether litigation is worthwhile.
qs: “A lot of what you pay the lawyer for is lawyers’ judgment,” said the lawyer from the HOA case.
“Knowing when to push, when not to push, what’s going to work with the judge, what’s not going to work with the judge, what’s a feasible argument, what’s not.”

“And right now it will do that and hallucinate case law. But even if it starts getting law correct, that doesn’t mean it can really make independent heuristic judgment on whether the case is still worthwhile.”

kp.k: Sanctions and disclosure requirements respond to AI misuse
kp.d: The article reports that some AI-reliant litigants face opposing counsel's fees, fines, dismissals and vexatious-litigant designations that generally require permission for future lawsuits. Interviewees also warn of reputational damage from public records. Some courts require disclosure of AI-generated documents, described as a limited response rather than a comprehensive solution.
qs: In addition to ending up saddled with the opposing council’s attorney fees, many of these AI-focused petitioners have faced court sanctions including expensive fines and harsh dismissals from fed-up judges.
Others have wound up being labelled vexatious litigants, which generally means that they now need to request permission to file future lawsuits.

Beyond sanctions, some courts that have encountered this issue have taken some limited steps to curb unwieldy AI lawsuits, for example requiring that all parties disclose when documents are AI-generated.

kp.k: Guided AI use may improve access to legal help
kp.d: The article acknowledges that most self-representation arises from need and that poor and marginalized people face serious barriers to counsel. Lou Rulli presents AI's ability to simplify procedures and support vital interests as an early-stage opportunity. Jennifer Gundlach reports observing successful self-represented use, particularly with informed legal-assistance guidance, and urges responsible experimentation rather than blanket discouragement.
qs: The vast majority of those who turn to self-representation do so purely out of need; that a new technology could serve as a democratizing force within the legal world, legal access advocates urge, is essential terrain to explore.
She shared that she’s seen first-hand self-represented folks find success with the help of the tech, particularly when chatbot use is coupled with informed guidance from organizations like hers.
“We have to be creative and forward-thinking in how to use this tool responsibly,” Gundlach said of generative AI.

kp.k: Beneficial use requires understanding AI's limitations
kp.d: An unnamed judge's dismissal order recognizes AI's potential to help self-represented litigants bring meritorious cases, while warning that requested responses may be generated without an arguable legal basis. The article's concluding distinction is between making litigation easier to initiate and making it advisable: lower production barriers do not establish merit or protect users from consequential litigation mistakes.
qs: But, he cautioned, “accessing any beneficial use of artificial intelligence requires carefully understanding its limitations.”

“For example, if merely asked to write an opposition to an opposing party’s motion or brief, or to respond to a court order, an artificial intelligence program is likely to generate such a response,” the order continues, “regardless of whether the response actually has an arguable basis in the law.”
“And just because the ‘can’ part has suddenly become a lot easier,” he added, “it doesn’t mean it’s still a good idea.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Landymore reports that generative AI amplifies burdensome self-represented litigation by making voluminous, superficially credible filings easy to produce; interviewed professionals contrast this with AI’s conditional potential to improve legal access.
pts.d: The author and interviewed lawyers describe chatbots as increasing the volume of filings, sustaining groundless legal theories, shifting substantial response costs onto opposing parties, and consuming court capacity. The author calls the presentation of flawed claims in authoritative legal language 'cogency-washing.' Interviewees argue that agreeable chatbots do not supply the independent judgment and realistic expectations that responsible lawyers provide, and that fabricated authorities are only one part of the problem. The local-government attorney explicitly suggests that accurate statements of law would not necessarily resolve the lack of judgment about whether litigation is worthwhile. The article also reports AI-associated harassment of lawyers, bar complaints, and sanctions against litigants. In contrast, Lou Rulli identifies an opportunity for AI to explain procedures and provide limited support to people without counsel; Jennifer Gundlach reports successful use by self-represented people, particularly alongside informed legal-aid guidance. These are claims about both unmediated reliance on chatbots and guided assistance, not a blanket claim that all self-represented AI use is harmful.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article relies on practitioner interviews, reviewed court filings, illustrative disputes, a contested lawsuit, and legal-access experts’ experience rather than systematic prevalence data or model benchmarks.
pts.d: Landymore says he interviewed lawyers and paralegals across specialties and reviewed documents from local, state, and federal courts; most interviewees remained anonymous. Examples include a Florida HOA dispute involving hundreds of pages of filings and escalating RICO allegations, ultimately dismissed with prejudice; a nearly 600-page complaint; and Ficarrotta’s account of a commissioner reviewing 500 pages of irrelevant AI-generated pleadings. Anonymous lawyers report costs rising from a historical approximately $2,000 to more than $20,000 in one dispute and from approximately $5,000 to more than $70,000 in another. These are case accounts, not measured average effects. A lawyer reports receiving more than 300 apparently AI-generated accusatory emails by January 2026. Nippon Life Insurance’s assertion that ChatGPT encouraged litigation over a settled claim and caused $300,000 in defense fees is presented as an allegation in its complaint, not an adjudicated finding; OpenAI denies the lawsuit’s merit. Rulli supplies legal-access expertise, while Gundlach supplies first-hand experience of successful assisted use. The article also quotes an unnamed judge’s order warning that generated responses need not have an arguable legal basis. It gives no representative incidence estimate, controlled comparison, or measured hallucination rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The harms are described as already occurring in 2025–2026; access benefits are both reported in current guided practice and framed as an early-stage opportunity without a specified forecast date.
pts.d: The Florida dispute began in early 2025; the harassment example resumed in 2025 and was described as continuing through January 2026. The article characterizes AI as amplifying an existing vexatious-litigation problem rather than creating it. Its negative claims concern especially high-volume, poorly grounded, uncritically relied-on chatbot output, not all AI-assisted legal work. Lawyers are also described as submitting fabricated case law, but the author distinguishes professional negligence from lay users’ misplaced belief that agreeable chatbots have validated their claims. The local-government attorney’s prediction that better legal accuracy may not provide independent judgment is conditional and undated. Rulli describes AI as early-stage, and Gundlach links observed benefits particularly to informed guidance. The quoted judicial order conditions beneficial use on understanding limitations. Fee recovery is sometimes possible but may be restricted by state statutes; some courts have introduced AI-disclosure requirements, described as limited measures rather than established solutions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Reported effects extend from self-represented litigants and their opponents to lawyers, court personnel, other court users, and people unable to obtain counsel.
pts.d: Self-represented parties gain a low-barrier means of drafting and filing but may pursue unsound claims and face fines, fee awards, dismissal, filing restrictions, and reputational harm. Opposing clients bear review and response costs; examples span HOA, collections, foreclosure, family, small-business, government, and insurance disputes. Ficarrotta highlights costs imposed on clients who are victims of intimate partner violence. Lawyers and paralegals face substantial additional work and sometimes personal accusations or bar complaints. Judges, commissioners, clerks, and staff attorneys must process filings and check purported authorities, while other litigants wait for attention on crowded dockets. These institutional burdens are distinct from the access-to-justice opportunity identified for poor and marginalized people with unmet civil legal needs: guided AI use could make procedures more understandable and support protection of important interests. The article does not predict quantified profession-wide employment changes or market-share shifts.
